The biggest ones are children, commitment, and finances.

This is a fundamental issue that can determine the success or failure of your relationship. You cannot really change someone's mind about whether or not they want children. If you think you can change their mind, you're mistaken. You need to look in the mirror and realize you are being unfair by not being honest with your partner. If you are both okay with saving for the future and being frugal, that's fine. If you both prefer to spend more on experiences now rather than retire a year earlier, that's fine too. There are some things that will reduce stress, like having a plan to reasonably cover unexpected expenses. But it's about being on the same basic wavelength. If one of you is a saver who likes to keep most of their income, and the other spends freely, there will be conflict. There are also different approaches to managing money. Will you combine everything into a shared account, keep some separate, or manage everything independently? IP lawyer is a broad term, often used to describe non-patent lawyers who work in intellectual property. Patent lawyer is a protected term for those who are registered to practice before the patent office. (Usually the state bar also protects the term, but I can't qualify every state does).

Patent lawyers are also known as patent prosecutors; they write patents and prosecute them before the patent office. They can do other things as well, but their jobs usually revolve around the patent office. All of them meet a set of requirements for the relevant patent office, which generally means they have at least a bachelor's degree in a field of science or engineering (not all STEM degrees are equal here as math degrees don't count, and not even all science and engineering degrees always count). Many have master's or PhDs in the field. (I was once in a PhD program some years ago).

Other types of IP lawyers do different work. For example, a patent litigator is someone whose work with patents is related to lawsuits involving patents. Some patent litigators are patent attorneys, but you're not required to be unless you're doing part of the litigation in front of the patent office.

IP litigator is more often used when the attorney works in the 'soft IP' field as well. That is, copyrights, trademarks, as well as more obscure areas like designs, rights of publicity, or boat bodies. Litigators are still individuals who are focused on lawsuits.

Now from what you've said about corporate or personal injury, those are different things. Personal injury work is litigation. Some litigators are just litigators. They handle all fields. But in IP, because of the time, cost, and expense usually involved in doing all the research, it tends to result in specialists who focus solely on IP litigation.

That said, litigation usually breaks into several different roles, with one that's fairly universal being the trial attorney. The type of attorney who goes in front of the jury isn't always the lead attorney. You want a trial attorney who knows how to connect with people. It's a very different skill and doesn't require a degree from a prestigious law school. (For example, in a famous defense team, one member had a degree from a mid-ranked law school, compared to much of the rest of the team who came from 'better schools', but that member had the knack with juries).

Many civil trial attorneys become hired guns who come in at the end of a big and complicated case. The truth is most cases don't go to trial, so having an experienced trial attorney running a lawsuit is often unnecessary. For civil trial attorneys, many may develop specialties but still branch out. A well-known former politician was most famous for his trial skills in medical malpractice cases against doctors whose mistakes in delivering a baby resulted in a child needing lifetime nursing care, but he also handled significant product liability cases. (He wrote a book about these and other cases). So doing all types of litigation is possible in trial.
